text.p: British building materials group Caradon Plc celebrated an 18 percent rise in 1996 profits on Wednesday by saying it planned to return 174 million pounds ($281.4 million) of its capital to shareholders.
Caradon shares rose 6.5 pence to 260 by 1135 GMT after the group said it would return cash for 10 percent of its market value in May following shareholder approval.
Shareholders are to be issued with a new class of "B" shares that they will be able to sell back to the company to raise cash.

Chief executive Peter Jansen said the group would still be able to afford further bolt-on acquisitions after the cashback and expressed interest in the U.S. and Germany, despite the difficult market there.

"We have enough financial firepower," Jansen said in a telephone conference call. "We've had a profit result at the top-end of expectations and better-than-expected cost reductions, so we are more than able to do this."
Pretax profits jumped to 178.2 million pounds before a 25.7 million pound exceptional loss related to disposals and a one-off six million pound charge for more cost-cutting programmes.
The strength of sterling last year knocked two million pounds off the profit-line.

Even so, underlying profits were at the top-end of market forecasts and the group delivered cost savings worth 66 million pounds. European non-core business disposals raised 220 million and the net cash inflow last year was 65 million. Shareholder funds rose to 586 million.
Continued sluggishness in European markets remained a problem. "1997 has started slowly, with trading in the early months generally below expectations," Jansen said in the results statement.

Britain was expected to show a recovery in the second quarter this year, but like the rest of the industry, Jansen did not see any rebound on the Continent until 1998. North America remained positive, however.

A divisional breakdown showed plumbing products saw flat sales of 387.9 million pounds, with profits up just one percent at 37.4 million. The profit line was hampered by a 4.5 million charge for the closure of a Cardiff bathroom facility, with the underlying performance up 13 percent.
Doors and windows saw sales of 561.1 million, up 15 percent, with profits swinging to a 20.1 million gains versus a 3.4 million loss, largely thanks to advances in North America.
Electrical product sales fell four percent to 301 million and profits fell 14 percent to 35.2 million. This was partly due to a poor market in Britain and the cost of new product launches.

Structural and engineering products sales were up four percent at 336.8 million and profits up eight percent to 22.3 million. Security and printing sales rose five percent to 211 million, with profits up 13 million to 42.8 million. ($ = 0.618 British Pounds)
